question: How do motorist and cyclist deaths compare year by year in NYC, 2013 to 2025?

options.metric: Annual number of recorded motorist deaths and cyclist deaths, each calculated as the sum of its corresponding *_killed column
options.denominator: None; these are counts of recorded people killed, not rates
options.grouping: Calendar year, with two series: motorist deaths and cyclist deaths
options.reason: Absolute annual death counts provide the most direct year-by-year comparison of the recorded fatality burden for each road-user group.
options.answer: Motorist deaths exceeded cyclist deaths in all 13 years, with 2025 totals of 81 and 23, respectively.
options.interpretation: This directly compares annual recorded death counts by summing number_of_motorist_killed and number_of_cyclist_killed over all police-reported NYC crash rows dated in each calendar year from 2013 through 2025, grouped into motorist and cyclist series; for example, 2020 recorded 139 motorist deaths and 29 cyclist deaths. Absolute counts are a defensible measure of recorded fatality burden, but they do not compare individual risk or adjust for motorist or cyclist exposure. The check shows all 13 years run from January 1 through December 31, with 0 NULL dates, 0 rows at the checked 1900/1970 date sentinels, and 0 missing values in either killed column in every year. I kept all eligible rows, and no outcome values were omitted for missingness.

options.metric: Annual number of recorded motorist deaths and cyclist deaths per 1,000 police-reported crash rows, calculated as the relevant *_killed sum divided by the year's crash-row count and multiplied by 1,000
options.denominator: Count of all police-reported NYC motor vehicle crash rows in each calendar year (not people, trips, miles, or road-user exposure)
options.grouping: Calendar year, with two series: motorist deaths per 1,000 crashes and cyclist deaths per 1,000 crashes
options.reason: Normalizing death counts by annual crash-record volume offers a useful comparison when the number of reported crashes varies substantially by year.
options.answer: This framing answers only part of the question: in 2023, the rates were 1.273 motorist deaths and 0.321 cyclist deaths per 1,000 reported crashes.
options.interpretation: This answers only part of the question by comparing the sum of each *_killed column divided by the annual count of all police-reported NYC crash rows and multiplied by 1,000, for crash dates in 2013–2025 inclusive, grouped by calendar year and road-user series; in 2023 the measures were 1.273 motorist deaths and 0.321 cyclist deaths per 1,000 crash rows. It is a defensible crash-volume-normalized measure, but it does not answer comparative individual risk because the data contain no motorist or cyclist exposure denominator. The largest neighboring-year denominator change was a decrease of 98,568 crash rows, from 211,486 in 2019 to 112,918 in 2020; a rise or fall in the per-crash measure across those years can result from that denominator shift and not from the death count, so compare the rates with that caution. All years are complete in the file, there are 0 NULL dates and 0 rows at the checked 1900/1970 date sentinels, and both killed columns have 0 missing rows in each year; I retained all eligible crashes in each denominator and no outcome values were omitted for missingness.

answer:
Motorist deaths exceeded cyclist deaths in every year from 2013–2025; in 2025, the recorded counts were 81 and 23, respectively.  
The per-1,000-crash framing answers only part of the question: in 2023, the rates were 1.273 motorist deaths and 0.321 cyclist deaths per 1,000 reported crashes, though rates can shift with crash-record volume.
